name: pinneapple_blender

children.name: pinneapple_blender.cycles
children.doc:
In-process Cycles renderer: build a small scene from NumPy arrays and render it with Blender's ``bpy`` module.

``render.py`` drives a separate Blender installation through a subprocess; this module uses the ``bpy`` Python
module directly (``pip install bpy``, which bundles Blender and Cycles), so a scene can be described from data in
the same process: surfaces from height grids, tubes along curves, point clouds, translucent planes, ribbons, text,
a camera, lights. Rendering is headless on the CPU.

    from pinneapple_blender.cycles import CyclesScene, available
    if available():
        sc = CyclesScene(resolution=(960, 540), samples=64)
        sc.add_surface(X, Y, Z, colors)               # (ny, nx) grids, colors (ny, nx, 3) in 0..1
        sc.add_plane(z=0.0, size=(10, 6), color=(0.1, 0.3, 0.6), alpha=0.35)
        sc.camera(location=(8, -9, 6), look_at=(0, 0, 0))
        sc.render("landscape.png")

``render_frames`` renders a sequence (the caller changes the scene between frames through a callback) and
``frames_to_video`` assembles them with ffmpeg.

classes.name: CyclesScene
classes.sig: (resolution = (960, 540), samples: int = 64, background = (0.97, 0.97, 0.96), ambient: float = 0.6, transparent: bool = False)
classes.doc:
A fresh Blender scene rendered with Cycles on the CPU.

``background`` is the world colour (also the ambient light, scaled by ``ambient``); ``samples`` the path-
tracing samples per pixel (denoised when Blender's OpenImageDenoise is available).

children.name: pinneapple_blender.export
children.doc:
Export a PINNeAPPle result (a point cloud + one or more scalar/vector
fields, optionally over several time steps) to a sequence of ``.ply``
files Blender can import natively (built-in importer, no add-on required
just to look at one frame) -- the PINNeAPPle-side half of the Blender
bridge; ``blender_addon/`` is the other half, running *inside* Blender.

Why PLY and not Alembic
------------------------
Alembic (the usual sim-to-DCC interchange format) would need the
``alembic``/``pyalembic`` Python bindings, which are not a normal
``pip install``-able package (built against Blender's/Maya's own bundled
libraries in practice) -- adding it as a dependency here would make this
module unusable for most people who don't already have a full VFX-pipeline
Python environment. PLY (a simple, well-specified, ASCII-or-binary mesh
format supporting arbitrary per-vertex properties, including colour) is
trivially writable with nothing beyond ``numpy``, and Blender has a
built-in PLY importer -- zero extra dependencies on either side of the
bridge, at the cost of "a directory of numbered files" instead of one
Alembic cache. See ``blender_addon/import_pinneapple_sequence.py`` for how
the numbered sequence becomes a Blender animation.

functions.name: write_ply
functions.sig: (path: str, points: np.ndarray, colors: np.ndarray | None = None, scalar_fields: dict[str, np.ndarray] | None = None) -> None
functions.doc:
Write a point cloud (no faces -- a vertex-only PLY, which Blender's
importer turns into a mesh with only vertices, ready for a Point Cloud
Visualizer-style geometry-nodes setup, or straightforward as a
particle/point render). ``colors``: (N,3) uint8 RGB, optional.
``scalar_fields``: extra named (N,) float properties beyond colour
(kept as raw values, not just their colour-mapped visualisation, so a
downstream Blender geometry-nodes setup can still access the real
numbers).

functions.name: export_scene
functions.sig: (points: np.ndarray, field: np.ndarray, out_dir: str, *, field_name: str = 'field', cmap: str = 'viridis', frame_index: int = 0, extra_fields: dict[str, np.ndarray] | None = None) -> str
functions.doc:
Export one frame (one time instant / one realisation) as
``<out_dir>/frame_<NNNN>.ply``. Call once per frame with increasing
``frame_index`` to build a sequence -- see
:func:`export_trajectory` for the common "I already have every
frame's arrays" case in one call.

``points``: (N, 3). ``field``: (N,) -- the scalar mapped to vertex
colour via ``cmap``. ``extra_fields``: additional (N,) arrays kept as
raw PLY vertex properties (not colour-mapped) for downstream use in
Blender (e.g. driving a geometry-nodes displacement).

functions.name: export_trajectory
functions.sig: (points: np.ndarray, fields_over_time: Sequence[np.ndarray], out_dir: str, *, field_name: str = 'field', cmap: str = 'viridis') -> list
functions.doc:
Export a whole sequence at once: ``points`` fixed (N, 3), one
``field`` array (N,) per frame in ``fields_over_time``. This is the
natural shape for a PINN surrogate's own output -- evaluate the model
at the same spatial points across a range of ``t`` values and pass the
resulting list of (N,) arrays straight in.

Returns the list of written file paths, in frame order.

children.name: pinneapple_blender.render
children.doc:
Subprocess bridge to a real local Blender installation -- same pattern
as ``cfd_formats.abaqus_reader.export_odb_fields``: never guess at
Blender's internals from outside, shell out to Blender's own bundled
Python (``blender --background --python <script>``) running genuine
``bpy`` code (``blender_addon/import_pinneapple_sequence.py``).

functions.name: build_scene
functions.sig: (ply_dir: str, *, output_blend: str | None = None, blender_executable: str = 'blender', timeout: int = 600) -> str
functions.doc:
Run Blender headless to import a ``.ply`` sequence (as written by
``pinneapple_blender.export``) into a scene, optionally saving it as a
``.blend`` file.

Requires a local Blender installation with ``blender`` (or
``blender_executable``) on ``PATH``.

Returns
-------
``output_blend`` if given, else ``ply_dir`` (the scene was built in
Blender's memory but not saved -- pass ``output_blend`` to keep it).

Raises
------
FileNotFoundError
    If ``blender_executable`` is not found on PATH.
RuntimeError
    If the Blender subprocess itself fails.

children.name: pinneapple_blender.step_extension.build
children.doc:
Build the Blender extension zip: ``python -m pinneapple_blender.step_extension.build --out dist [--wheels]``.

The zip holds the extension, a copy of :mod:`pinneapple_design.geometry.brep` under ``vendor/brep`` (so Blender needs
no PINNeAPPle install) and, with ``--wheels``, the wheels of smlibpy, mapbox-earcut and scipy for every platform
Blender ships on, listed in the manifest so Blender installs the right ones (Blender bundles numpy).
Install the zip with Edit > Preferences > Get Extensions > Install from Disk, or
``blender --command extension install-file -r user_default <zip>``.

functions.name: download_wheels
functions.sig: (dest: Path, python: str = '3.11', platforms = PLATFORMS, packages = WHEELS) -> list[Path]
functions.doc: pip-download one wheel per package and platform (no dependencies: Blender bundles numpy).

functions.name: build
functions.sig: (out: str | Path, wheels: bool = False, python: str = '3.11') -> Path
functions.doc: Write ``pinneapple_step-<version>.zip`` into ``out`` and return its path.

children.name: pinneapple_blender.step_extension.core
children.doc:
The part of the extension that needs no Blender: the library, the body cache, diagnostic colours and the
``MeshData`` export. Everything here works on numpy arrays and :class:`TessMesh` objects.

functions.name: brep
functions.doc: The library's ``brep`` package: the installed PINNeAPPle, or the copy the build put next to this file.

functions.name: bodies
functions.doc: The exact bodies of a STEP file, read once per session.

functions.name: colours
functions.sig: (values: np.ndarray, mode: str = 'sequential', clip_percentile: float = 98.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
RGB in [0, 1] per value. ``sequential`` maps the [min, p] range on a viridis ramp; ``diverging`` centres zero
(blue negative, red positive) and scales by the ``clip_percentile`` of |value|; ``gray`` maps [0, 1] to grey.

functions.name: diagnostic
functions.sig: (body, mesh, mode: str, *, stripes: int = 16, eye = None) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc:
Per-vertex values, their RGB colours and a summary for one of :data:`DIAGNOSTICS` on ``mesh`` (a
:class:`TessMesh` of ``body``). Curvatures are in 1/m and 1/m^2.

functions.name: write_meshdata
functions.sig: (mesh, path: str, name: str = '') -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Write the arrays of ``MeshData`` (vertices and faces in metres, face normals) and the body face of each
triangle to ``path`` (``.npz``), with a ``.json`` summary next to it. Load with
``MeshData(**{k: d[k] for k in ("vertices", "faces", "normals")})`` where ``d = np.load(path)``.

optionally build/save a Blender scene from it via a real local Blender
installation (``render.py``, subprocess bridge to Blender's own ``bpy``,
mirroring the ``cfd_formats.abaqus_reader`` ``.odb`` bridge pattern).
